utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We will continue with the evidence of Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Lukic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There were two matters from yesterday that you thought you might be able to assist further with this morning. One was the question whether the constitution of the Republic of Serbia dealt at all with the role of the Serbian authorities in controlling the border area. Are you able to help further on that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia placed within its jurisdiction inter alia border crossing and the control of circulation of trade, services, and passenger traffic across the border. The control of the circulation of goods and services was carried out by a federal organisation. It was called the Federal Customs Office. Other passenger traffic across the border at organised border crossings was controlled by the Ministries of the Interior of the two member republics at the border crossings that were set up in their territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to identify any provision in the constitution of the Republic of Serbia that deals with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to you yesterday what the mechanism was in case any of the functions that were envisaged to be performed by the federal government is not done in accordance with the federal law on the implementation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That meant that the regulations in place for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that were in place and that were applicable to this area were to be implemented by the relevant organs of the member republics. So that was the decision that was up to the constitutional legislator, who when the federal law on the implementation of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was passed, put in place this kind of a situation in this area or this kind of a mechanism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that give the president of the FRY authority over the MUP so far as it related to persons crossing the border?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of authority did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Command authority. In other words, the ability to take decisions that would affect -- directly affect the activities of the MUP to protect the integrity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably on the military regulations there should have been some kind of cooperation envisaged between the republics and also between the military and police forces of the federal state and the respective forces of the member republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you have is a federal task being carried out through necessity by a republican organ in circumstances where there's a threat to the security of the state because of terrorist activity and unauthorised crossing of the border, and I'm wondering how constitutionally that affected the relationship between the president of the FRY and the MUP, and I was hoping you as a constitutional expert might be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for explicit provisions about that, there are none in any of the constitutions, I believe, because the minister of the interior of each member republic is responsible for the work of his ministry on the one hand, and to the representative bodies of the member republics, and on the other, the government of the member republic directs the work of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the other matter that was left outstanding is related to this, and that was about the -- the basis for Milosevic to reach an agreement with Holbrooke about the reduction of the numbers of MUP forces in Kosovo. Now, what was his constitutional authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that I answered to a similar question you asked yesterday, and in my answer I referred to the relevant articles of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, taking as my starting point what I always have to bear in mind as a lawyer and that is the fact that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was an entity under international law as an independent and sovereign state and that there are organs of international relations and that it had the authority to enter treaties under international law, whereas its member republics did not have those powers. I referred to -- let me repeat now once again but I think that it is in the transcript from the session yesterday, I think that it was the same question, and in the end I said that this was possible because the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia represents the country in the country and abroad, whereas the president of the republic as the head of state, on the other hand, not only in accordance with the general international law but also under the Vienna Conventions on treaty law, is one of the bodies that has this contractual -- that embodies this contractual power of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did deal with the matter yesterday, but at the end you said: "How this agreement was reached, I don't know, but I'm trying to see whether it can be brought into line with constitutional norms," and I thought that you were going to be more specific today. It's one thing, though, for a president to represent a state in a formal sense, and it's another thing for the president to be able to commit the state to an agreement or a policy or whatever. Now, are you saying that it was within the power of the president of the FRY, in terms of the constitution, to actually reach an agreement with Holbrooke? Never mind the government, prime minister, or anyone else, it was within Milosevic's power?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this again. It appears to me that I have answered your question now how this agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can answer that one yes or no. Are you saying it was within his constitutional power, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To enter an agreement because he represents the country, yes, he did. It was within his power. A lot of things have changed under international law, so there may be this idea that agreements are reached by persons, not by entities. I cannot view this as a lawyer in this way, but in the country where you come from, no law can be made valid unless it is first approved by the Queen with her private council. First it has 700 members, and now there are only two secretaries, one secretary and two members. So without that, no law is law in your country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be, Professor, but it's not assisting my understanding of the position in Yugoslavia. I just want to be clear that Milosevic could commit the government of Yugoslavia to the obligations he entered into with Holbrooke. That was within his constitutional power.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an agreement could have been entered into by the president of the republic, federal prime minister and minister of foreign affairs. Those are the representative organs, organs that undertake obligations on behalf of the state and create rights and powers for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect, you're not answering my question. I want to know whether the president on his own, without reference to anyone else, was capable of entering into an agreement with Holbrooke in the terms in which he did committing the government of Yugoslavia to that agreement. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say this again with all due respect that I can only give you the answer that I've already given and that according to my legal knowledge and my legal approach I can actually give you. These are hypothetical questions. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean hypothetical? Milosevic did enter into agreement with Holbrooke about the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a question of this kind. I hope that the translation was correct. If Milosevic -- I'm quoting back to you what you said. If Milosevic entered into an agreement with Holbrooke without asking anyone whether he could commit the federal government to actually implement this agreement, I think this is a hypothetical question and I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know that the facts are different from that? Tell us your -- tell us your understanding of the factual position then, because our understanding is that he is the person on one view of the evidence in the case that entered an agreement with Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you may know that. I don't know anything about those facts. I really don't know anything about those facts. It's possible that you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not prepared to enter into arguments with you from the Bench. Your job here is to answer my questions to the best of your ability. Now, I am putting a position to you, and I want an answer to that situation, and that is that -- and the question is whether Milosevic on his own had authority under the constitution to enter into the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement and to commit the government of Yugoslavia to that agreement, and I expect you can answer that yes or no and then I'll follow it up with other questions.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what other organs apart from the three that I mentioned could enter into agreements of that kind. The president of the Republic of Serbia could not do that because Serbia was merely a federal unit. It did not have the contractual capacity. Under the Vienna Conventions -- Convention on international treaty law the federal units do not have this kind of capacity to enter into any contracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where does the president of the republic come into this? I'm not asking you about that. Please do not try to divert attention from the issue. The issue is a very simple one. The extent of the power of the president of the FRY to enter into an agreement he entered into with Holbrooke. Now, did he have power under the constitution to do that? And if you're not going to answer me, then we'll move on and we'll regard you as unable to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered you to the best of my ability as to the legal position. Who else could have entered into such an agreement apart from the head of state, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, or the federal Prime Minister, because Yugoslavia at that time was seen as a single entity under international law. After all, the member republics could enter into international treaties in affairs that were within their purview but through federal organs, to the organs of the federal state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm just looking for one of your earlier answers so that I can have it retranslated. I would like CLSS to provide a formal interpretation of page 5, lines 16 to 20. You earlier have been translated as saying that the people who could enter into such agreement were the president of the federal government, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and the president of the republic and that has partly contributed to this exchange. You've now clarified the third person as the prime minister of the federal republic.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this is lack of understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Sorry, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just different terminology. I am talking about the president of the federal republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think so. You had -- it may be a mistranslation. We'll get it clarified in due course.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second is the prime minister of the federal government, and the third person is the Minister of Foreign Affairs. After all, under international law and national law there is the instrument of ratification, because those persons conduct talks. They do not get any special authority for any such talks, but most of the treaties and contracts have to be gone over and ratified at a later stage. Not all of them, but for the most part yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, what do you know about the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very, very little about this agreement because I did not deal with that specifically, and it was not part of my expert report. All I know comes from the minutes that were submitted to me yesterday by the Prosecution. I have no other knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What minutes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I was given by the Prosecution to go over it during the break yesterday. That's the only document that I was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just finally on this point, what provision of the FRY constitution is it that gives the president of the FRY the authority to enter into such negotiation? Is it Article 77 or is it some other article?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Article 96, paragraph 1, where it says that the president of the republic shall represent the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia at home and abroad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's it?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In my opinion that's it, because in our language the word to represent has that meaning in constitutional law and international law related to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if -- if you can then put a badge of international or foreign relations on any issue, it then falls within the area of responsibility of the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Foreign policy is within the purview of the federal government as can be seen from paragraph 1, Article 99, but international representation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which includes the capacity to sign treaties regardless of any other mechanism of ratification or anything else of the sort is within the purview of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, of the prime minister of the federal government, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can turn now to the appointment of Mr. Sainovic to deal with matters affecting Kosovo. What influence do you think it is appropriate for the president of the FRY to have on that appointment, again within the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know about the duties and obligations that Mr. Sainovic as the federal deputy prime minister in relation to Kosovo stems from yesterday's document which was given to me to read and where in one place I found mention of a body which was in charge of Kosovo, or tasked with the issue of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've provided the report that makes it clear that the prime minister would appoint the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To what extent would you consider it appropriate for the president to bring influence to bear on the prime minister in relation to that appointment?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All organs have to cooperate among themselves to work, exchange ideas. Contact between the highest constitutional authorities is not prohibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So would it be appropriate for the president to make suggestions to the prime minister about the tasks he should assign to a deputy prime minister?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in any case they have to exchange opinions. Opinions are also exchanged about people, but the appointment is in the hands of the federal government. The predominant position of the federal prime minister means that he decides what tasks a deputy prime minister will carry out within the sphere of competence of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. There's no -- there are no tricks in these questions. You and I both know there are circumstances in which it's inappropriate for organs to communicate with each other. For example, it's inappropriate for the government to communicate with a judge in relation to his activities. So it's not a simple matter of everybody must cooperate. There are constitutional provisions which regulate how organs relate to one another, and within that I entirely accept that there must in some circumstances be discussion and so on. I just want to know what is right and what's wrong in relation to influence in terms of the constitution. So let me make it more specific. Is it appropriate within the constitution for the president of the FRY to say to the prime minister, "I want you to appoint X, Mr. X, as deputy prime minister"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? It may be an issue of wording, of the way this is styled, but I don't see why the president of the republic should not consult with the prime minister, because they belong to the same type of organ. These are organs of executive government, the executive branch of government, and the largest part of the executive branch of government is wielded by the government and a very small part by the president. So one can conclude that the federal government is almost the exclusive representative or almost the exclusive body implementing executive power. So this kind of communication and cooperation is normal in our country. In the USA the president of the republic is not allowed to participate in any way with the two representative houses in their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, really -- I'm afraid it doesn't help us, Professor, to travel to the USA on this either, or for me to travel home, for that matter. Let me read to you from the former Prime Minister Bulatovic's book. "Milosevic's second request was to charge Nikola Sainovic, Deputy prime minister, with running political activities related to obligations concerning Kosovo and Metohija." Now, my question's a simple one. Is it okay for the president to do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the scope of communication with the federal government the giving of proposals is normal. It's the federal government that decides -- or, rather, the prime minister of the federal government, in this case Mr. Bulatovic, is the one who decides whether he will take on board this proposal or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is the answer yes, it's okay?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not prohibited by the constitution. This kind of communication and cooperation among organs is not prohibited by the constitution. Everything else is psychology, and -- well, it says here request or proposal. This can -- request can be translated into the Serbian language in various ways. The manner of communication among organs not prescribed by legislation. There are no magic formulas either, oaths and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the transcript, I believe the witness started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From the transcript, Your Honour, page 12, line 14 I believe the witness said "yes" in Serbian. If we can just have CLSS check that out, at the beginning of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is pointing out that -- that where I asked you if the answer was, yes, it's okay, you actually said, "Yes, in Serbia it's not prohibited by the constitution," but I'm not asking you about Serbia. I'm asking you about the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He didn't say "in Serbia." In Serbian he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Serbian. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Do you know whether Milosevic and Bulatovic were members of the same political party?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume they were not, because Mr. Bulatovic is from Montenegro, and at that time there was no federal political party, at least not in parliament in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know whether they shared the same political philosophy?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say that at present. Their political thoughts and philosophies is something I have not made a study of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These events that I've been referring to, the charging of Mr. Sainovic with responsibilities for Kosovo, happened at the time you were the Foreign Minister of Republika Srpska. Sorry, Deputy Foreign Minister.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events occurred at a later date. I was the Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs of Republika Srpska until early January 1998 when a new government was formed and this ministry ceased to exist. All affairs concerning the cooperation of Republika Srpska with international organisations and other states were taken over by the prime minister within the scope of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was a single legal entity at the time. So I was then no longer the deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of expressions you use in your report is judicial autonomy. What do you mean which judicial autonomy of a province?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This expression means that a province has its own courts and that trials, as a rule, or legal proceedings end in the province and that the courts of the state, whether the state is a federal unit, so it's a kind of internal state or federal unit, as a rule cannot decide on the judgements of the highest court or courts in an autonomous province, or as is said in my language, a unit of political territorial autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the autonomous provinces had their on constitutional courts as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Under the constitution of 1974, the autonomous provinces also had their own constitutional courts...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these existed until when?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They existed in formal terms until the constitution of 1990 entered into force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were they abolished both in Kosovo and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normative terms, yes, they were abolished both in Kosovo and Vojvodina. Under the constitution the federal -- of Serbia under the constitution of Serbia in normative legislative terms such courts exist neither in the autonomous province of Kosovo nor in the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could deal with that question again. There's been a technical hitch in the recording of that answer. I asked you whether they had their own constitutional courts and you said they had under the constitution of 1974, and then there was a question about the period of time that these operated. Could you deal with that again.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional -- or, rather, constitutional courts do not Exist in either of the two provinces under the constitution of Serbia from 1990, because according to that constitution, both provinces have the same legal constitutional position. In other words, in normative terms there is no difference between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When they -- when they did exist, did they have the final say on constitutional interpretation? Was there no further right of appeal beyond there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When answering this question it's very important to bear in mind what kind of constitutional issues could come up before the constitutional courts of the provinces. These were only those issues that concerned the constitutionality and legality -- or, rather, the constitutionality of laws and the constitutionality and the legality of other legal provisions, and there was a special category of legal documents called general acts of self-management which were enacted in the province. So those courts evaluated whether these documents and this legislation was in compliance with the constitution of the province. As regards the constitutionality and legality of this legislation and its harmonisation with the constitution of the federal state, if there was a claim that they violated that constitution, then if proceedings were instituted not as an appeal or as a legal remedy in relation to a decision handed down by the provincial Constitutional Court, but if an issue was raised before the federal Constitutional Court initially, then that court would decide on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why did these courts have to be abolished?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to be abolished because under the constitution of 1990 the highest constitutive act was not the constitution but the statute in the provinces, and there are really no examples where an autonomous province had its own Constitutional Court anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is -- is the difference between constitution and statute here a semantic difference or is there some crucial distinction between the two?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I think there was a question about that, and that was that within the scope of the principles of the federal constitution of 1974 the provinces had competence, competence jurisdiction, which means that they could decide on their organisation. Now a different kind of organisation of provinces was envisaged, and the limits of that organisation are represented by the constitution and laws of the Republic of Serbia. So is it's not just a rhetorical difference. The difference is in the general position of the province, and in my expert report and in answer to the Prosecution question, I said that apart from two or three major issues the republics were similar to federal units. In fact, they were equal to federal units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what -- what in practice was the difference in the organisation of the provinces following the amendments of 1989 -- or, rather, 1990?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provinces had their representative bodies which enacted the statute and decisions, but they could not pass laws as the legal literature in my area calls them primordial laws because social relations are primarily regulated bylaws, and the legislator decided what part of normative government would be delegated to the provinces. The province had its executive organ but it no longer had its Supreme Court, its Constitutional Court. In other words, it did not have full judicial autonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your answer a moment ago is translated as saying, "I said that apart from two or three major issues the republics were similar to federal units." Should that be the provinces?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provinces. That's what I said, the provinces resembled federal units except into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a translation problem. It's not your responsibility. It's a notorious fact of experience that when you give power in any area of life to someone and you then try to take it away, it's likely to cause difficulty. If you give someone a pay rise and then decide to change your mind and take it off them, it's likely to create great disappointment at the very least, and I think you accepted in your evidence that in a number of areas the degree of autonomy that had existed for the provinces was diminished as the result of the reforms at the turn of this decade. Why, as far as you're been able to discover, were these changes made?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it's well known that what you said is so. There's an old saying: God grant that you may first have something and then not having if you wish someone ill. As a lawyer the main question is how an autonomy comes into existence and whether it's an acquired right that cannot be changed. In order to create an autonomy only the state has competence, competence authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. I don't think that's the issue, with respect. I have little doubt at the moment that you're right, that it's open to -- in theory, for the body with the ultimate say to make changes. That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you whether your researches have established why this was done.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me another question just about -- just when I was about to enter into that. The reasons for those changes, as far as I know, lay in the following: Serbia was blocked as far as enacting laws is concerned under Article 300 and 301, principally Article 300 of the constitution of Serbia which were laws which, as the constitutional norm of the laws of Serbia stated were applied throughout the territory of the republic. And furthermore, Serbia was the sole republic or federal unit of the then state of existence which could not change its constitution on its own. It was a truly intricate procedure. So this kind of situation, constitutional situation in Serbia led to a series of problems in the functioning of Serbia. And as far as I know, there were some major unrests in Kosovo province, not in Vojvodina province, just prior to the beginning of what was called by the Badinter Commission the dissolution of Yugoslavia in which it was demanded that Kosovo become a federal unit within the composition of Yugoslavia. To the best of my knowledge those were the actual reasons for this change in the constitution, and it was allowed to go through with the changes in the SFRY constitution and the amendments dating back to 1988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And again I can understand that -- that there can be deadlock and difficulty in government and that might explain constitutional changes, but I think you also said that the result was that there were four or five circumstances in which the actual autonomy of the province was diminished. Can you tell me what these four or five circumstances were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. First of all, the province did not have its constitution or a province did not, and its organisation was prescribed by the constitution of Serbia, the basic foundations, and that was a code in Article 111 where it is stated which organs a province has. So the province could not enact laws. The republic enacted regulations for the execution of its laws, and Yugoslavia at that time had an extremely difficult, complicated situation -- or, rather, system which proved to be unsuccessful in implementing federal laws in federal units and autonomous provinces, and similarly a catastrophically unsuccessful system in enacting the laws of Serbia on the territory of the provinces. Not all the laws were enacted. All laws that were applied throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia, in fact, and in the functioning of each state they are extremely serious problems. And finally the destiny and fate of that Yugoslavia shows the contribution of such a complicated system of carrying out the laws and enacting the laws and putting them into practice by one unit down to a lower unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is some evidence before us of changes in the arrangements for regulating contractual relations. Do you know about that change?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what change you have in mind and what period of time, what act, what contractual relations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you could look please at P858 and if we can see on the screen amendment 32. You see that amendment now on the screen. Can you tell me what the effect of that was, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part of the amendment are you thinking of in amendment 32?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All of it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are different points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would just like to know what the effect of that amendment in its entirety was.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To what? Position of whom? In relation to whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to Kosovo. Did this -- this is an amendment which holds true, as far as I can see, for the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and it says that it regulates obligations and contractual relations, determines condition for building, finance, management, use of housing, the transactions involved in flats and residential buildings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the constitution of Serbia in force at the time now, and they were very long constitutions with 400-odd articles. So I don't know all of them off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking you because they're very difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to see what this regulates. Legalese at the time was very complicated, the language used in law, because it had a lot of elements that were not conducive to law, but that was what the times were like. Reading this, reading the text of this amendment, I can't really -- I really can't answer your question because that is legal norm enacted as a general one to be applied on the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia, and I can't make any conclusions as to how it would influence the position of Kosovo. And ultimately all these amendments that you're showing me now were the subject of assessments by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, the amendments that I can't remember now when the constitutional decision was passed and its number, but these amendments having to do with the provinces were assessed by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia positively, that is to say that they were in conformity with the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure they were, but it's not the issue that I'm exploring, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm giving you an answer to the best of my ability as I understood your question and as far as I am able to organise my thoughts in responding to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what needs to be done, actually, is to make a direct comparison with Article 299 of the previous constitution to see whether it affected Kosovo at all, and it may be that it didn't. I simply wanted to know if you knew the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 299 competencies are -- and the functions of the Republic of Serbia are regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, let me repeat, the constitution of Serbia at the time had 430 or 40-odd articles, the Vojvodina constitution 420, the Kosovo constitution 400-odd again, and I don't have them before me here. I left them in my hotel room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we move then to amendment 33, which is one that is discussed in your report. It's on the next page. Now, this is one that I think you do accept affected Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it refers to Article 300 and in part 423, I don't have the text of the constitution of Serbia in front of me, but probably in a way it does because this regulates -- this amendment regulates the competencies of the Republic of Serbia as applied uniformly to the entire territory. But it's far too long, as you can see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know whether these amendments altered the regime for property rights in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if it did, you may be able to assist in this. If it did, can you think of a reason why it was necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. I don't have the factual knowledge for that. And as I lived in Sarajevo, a different federal unit at the time, I really wasn't familiar with the reasons, all the reasons for all the amendments contained in this constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this may be a rather technical matter but it's required, I think, for the sake of clarification. On page 12 of your report, in the English version, which -- there is a paragraph which begins -- in the English it's about -- it's just over two-thirds of the way down: "According to the 1968 constitutional amendments..." do you have that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "The provinces in addition to the federation and the republics were within their rights and duties made responsible for the discharge of tasks and duties on their respective territories which under the federal contusion fall within the exclusive rights and duties of the federation." Now, that seems contradictory and here contradictory but it may be meant to be. Can you explain that sentence?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you just allow me a moment to find that portion in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 17 if I might be of assistance. Page 17, second paragraph in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's not contradictory. It isn't contradictory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you explain with --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- an example?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not going to be able to explain with an example, but I'll tell you what it is about. The system of distribution of competencies under the 1974 constitution knew certain -- recognised certain competencies of the federal state which -- legal competencies which belonged to the exclusive competencies of the federal state because its laws in those areas, the federal units, were not able to enact. So their participation in legislative authority in those areas was excluded. However, the very complicated system of enforcing federal laws which in the vast majority were not enforced by the federal organs themselves because there were just a few federal organisations organised throughout the territory of Yugoslavia, the customs organisations, the army and so on, very few of them, they carried out federal regulations throughout the country, whereas the vast majority of the regulations were enforced by the federal units themselves, which implied under certain conditions, bylaws and executive provisions, so that was a complicated system of division of authority for -- between the federal authorities and the federal units. And with the constitution of 1968 the provinces as well became -- to all intents and purposes had the authorisation of carrying out federal laws, enforcing federal laws for which the federal state -- from the competence of the federal state on the territory of their -- of the provinces, they were responsible for that and made responsible for that enforcement. So that is the meaning of it and there is indeed no contradiction there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can you give me an example? Bring it to life.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot do that. I can't give you an example. I know the systemic solutions there, but any federal -- if you take any federal law which was not enforced by federal organisations but was enforced by the republics and provinces, you'd have to take that in order to conclude that for enforcement of such federal laws it was the provinces who were responsible for that. They were complicated formulations and complicated language was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't believe you live in such an ivory tower that you don't -- you're unable to give an example of this. Your inability as someone familiar with the area who lived there to give an example suggests that this is theoretical and didn't exist in practice. There must be something that you can think of that fell within this --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot at this point in time. Let me be very frank. Nothing comes to mind from the laws at this particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you turn to page 19 of the English of your report, and hopefully Mr. Petrovic will assist me again. And if you look at the large paragraph in the bottom half of the English certainly version, it begins "Being constituent elements of the federation ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is on page 26 of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could go, Professor, to the end of that paragraph, about five lines from the bottom. "On the other hand even though existing within the composition of the republic, the autonomous provinces were not represented as such in the republican organs, although some republican organs had members by virtue of office, that means that the provinces as such had greater rights in the federation than in the republic. Can you there give examples of a republican organ in which the province was not represented dealing with an area of activity where somehow or other the province by direct representation in the federation achieved some additional autonomy or power? And again it's very theoretical paragraph and I would like to try and put meat on the skeleton.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The provinces were represented in the federal organs as were -- as federal units with certain differences. The province was represented in the Presidency of the Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for example, and in corresponding fashion, and the formulations are very complicated bearing in mind national representation, equal representation of the republics, provinces and so on was represented in the Federal Executive Council as well as it was represented in both Chambers of the SFRY Assembly. Truth to tell, the number of delegates from there was about a third or a little more, depending on the council, less than was the representation of the federal units within the federal council and council of chambers and provinces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article -- that was that kind of representation. It had equal legal consequences regardless of the fact that it was a little lower than the equal representation of the federal units that they enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is more related to the end of your paragraph where you explain that the provinces were not represented in the republican organ. Can you give me examples of this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As such they weren't represented in the republican -- represented as they were in the federation in the republican ones, although my aim was here to indicate the unusualness of that position. That was my object, to show how far that position went beyond everything that was known in constitutional law and comparative law with respect to autonomy. So my aim there in that place was to show how they were represented in the federal state, for example, and were not represented in the federal unit and to show in a way how they were skipped over, the levels were skipped over, as one of the elements, let me put it this way, of the distortion of their position, how distorted their position was if we bear in mind the average understanding of the concept of autonomy. Because you don't get to autonomy of its own but by comparing it to other forms, well-known forms of autonomy. So that was the object of my observation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is just a general comment in case you want to make your own comment on it, but have not -- have not the last 25 years or so of history told us that there's no limit to the forms of autonomy that can be granted in areas of the world and that it's rather short-sighted to confine attention to one or two well-recognised formats?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could look at this problem in that way, but no autonomy can be such as to jeopardise the normal functioning of the state wherein it is situated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That's a rather different point. Can you give me an example where the provinces had members by virtue of office participating in republican organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is stated here members by virtue of their position. That's conditionally speaking, because every time the members of the federal government were appointed care was taken to ensure that -- or, rather, when courts, member of the courts were appointed, then care was taken to ensure that people from the provinces were represented. There were no explicit norms to that effect, but this was something that was taken care of. That was something that was taken into account. Of course the organs that are -- where people are appointed on the basis of direct elections, that I'm not talking about because they're representative organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're -- the wording of your report is: "Some republican organs had members by virtue of office." Now, what -- give me an example of that so that I can try to understand it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is in quotation marks in the version that I have, which means that this is not the true representation such as we have when an autonomous unit is represented in the federal unit, but we're talking about the representation of the people from the provinces in the courts of the republic and other organs in the republic. But there were no norms to that effect. What I wanted to show here is that when the province became an element of the federation, in a way was removed from the constitutional system of Serbia. There were members of the Constitutional Court, Judges of the Constitutional Court of the Supreme Court, ministers, deputy ministers who were from Kosovo and Metohija and from the province. That's what I meant when I wrote this. And since this is in quotation marks, it means -- how should I put it? If you put it in quotation marks then you're talking about some kind of a para-institution or para-instrument, something that was applied in practice but did not really -- was not really legislated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So these are people who held positions as ministers, deputy ministers, judges of the Constitutional Court in Serbia, in the republic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After your -- your quotation marks are then expanded upon to say: "On the basis of their positions held in the province." Now, that's what I'm asking about. What position would a person hold in the province that led to him holding a position in the republic? It's your words.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm explaining to you why this is written here. Some of these elements were present in the position of the presidents of the presidencies in both provinces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's take, for example, a judge of the Constitutional Court in Serbia. What position in Kosovo that he held would lead to him being appointed a judge of the Constitutional Court in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such position. He was not a judge of some court in Kosovo and then that would mean that he was by virtue of this office a judge in the court of Serbia. He was elected because the representation of the provinces was something that was taken into account to make sure that they were represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's look at a government official, a minister, a deputy minister. Give me an example of one who held a position in Serbia because he held a particular position in Kosovo. Can you give me an example of such a position leading to appointments in --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just with the representatives of the provinces in the Presidency of Serbia. As for the rest, it was the principle whereby care was taken to ensure that representatives from the province were there, were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know the way in which the Supreme Defence Council operated?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know its composition?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the explicit provision in the constitution stipulating that the president of the federal republic and the presidents of the two republics were members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you express an opinion on the role to be played by the republican presidents in the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I did not look at the Rules of Procedure governing the work of that body, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one specific question then. Have you heard the term "Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this constitutional system I never heard this term. That is a term used at the times of the Communist revolution and from the national -- the war of national liberation. I think it was used in the previous system, but in the current constitutional system I have never encountered the term "Supreme Command." And I couldn't find a body under that name in any legal source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If I tell you that -- that General Ojdanic used the expression "Supreme Command" as a current expression in relation to activities in Kosovo, would you be able to tell us what the Supreme Command was? Do you have any understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely none, because General Ojdanic, with all due respect, is not a drafter of the constitution or a legislator. I cannot find any such body in the provisions of the federal constitutions and the provisions of the law dealing with issues of defence and military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You could perhaps have a look at 3D728. Page 3 in English. You'll see the comments attributed to General Ojdanic. This is a briefing of the Supreme Command Staff on the 11th of April, 1999. Does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean anything to me in the sense of my expert report as regards the legal provisions regulating defence and military issues. This don't mean anything to me because there are no provisions about this organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have to have a break at this stage. I have very little else to ask you, but I will do that after the break. That will be for half an hour. Again if you would please leave with the usher. We'll see you at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to return to the question of the Supreme Command, Professor, and we take you first of all to page 9 of the second part of your report, the part dealing with the federal structure or the federal organs, and you have of a section (G), relations between the Federal Cabinet, the Yugoslav army, and the supreme military council. I think that should be translated Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's at page 13 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. In that section (G) the last paragraph deals with the Supreme Defence Council. You tell us its composition and then you say, "The president of the republic commands the Yugoslav army in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council." What I'd like to ask you is what is the role of the republican presidents in the Supreme Defence Council as you understand that provision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presidents of the member republics are members of the Supreme Defence Council. In my analysis, I didn't go beyond the legal regulations concerning this issue, and that means that I analysed the law on the army of Yugoslavia and the law on defence. In these provisions the manner in which this organ is to work is not mentioned, and that is why beyond stating that they are members of this organ, I cannot say anything about the functioning of this organ because the topic of my expert report was to determine the legal relations between the Supreme Defence Council and the federal government. My analysis indicates that there were no legal relations between the two and that the federal government did not have any authority over the Supreme Defence Council. That was the subject of my analysis, because the whole expert report is entitled "The position of the federal government within the constitutional system," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you are an expert familiar with the constitutions that concern us, and what I'd now like to ask you is -- is should we regard the three members of the Supreme Defence Council as being of equal status?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is a collegiate organ it means that one person is a chairman or the president and the others are members. Now, as to the way in which the vote was taken, that's not something I can tell you about because I didn't analyse the rules of procedure. The laws that I looked at do not stipulate that. The only provision that does, conditionally speaking, talk about the way in which this organ worked, that's Article 41 of the Law on Defence that stipulates that the president of the Supreme Defence Council shall take care of implementing the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. Other provisions about the way in which this organ worked and which decisions were taken are not contained in those laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be we could look at Articles 40 and 41 of the Law on Defence. That's P1874. Is that the Law on Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the reference should be to the law on VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think you may be looking for P985, the Law on Defence. Article 41 talks about the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. This -- what's on the screen is the law on the VJ, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From 1991, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- Mr. Zecevic, what is P1874?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 1874 is the Law on Defence of Republic of Serbia of 1991 which ceased to exist after some time, and after the creation of the federal republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, indeed. Sorry, it is my mistake. It should be P985. Now, if you look at Article 41, you'll see that it sets out the things that the Supreme Defence Council should do and then says that the president shall ensure implementation of the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, and you can take it that the President of the Supreme Defence Council was the president of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's implied by the constitutional provision establishing the composition of this organ. It's not usual for constitutional provisions to be repeated in the legislation, although it often happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you -- would you expect the members of the Supreme Defence Council to have equal status in dealing with the items set out in Article 41?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If equal status means the work of the organ and participation in its work, of course. Decisions have to be made according to the rules of procedure of this organ. So conditionally speaking, it's an equal position except for what the president of this council does as someone who convenes sessions, proposes the agenda, makes sure the decisions are implemented and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you're a constitutional expert. What was the reason for having the presidents of the member republics as members of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I'm not familiar with the reasons. I can only assume that the nature of federal relations influenced the formation of this kind of Supreme Defence Council as an organ which has only these powers in the system of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there would appear to be two ways of reaching a determination, and perhaps you'll tell me if there are others. One would be by voting and therefore by majority, and the other would be by consensus. Are there any other ways?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can speak theoretically about the way decisions are made, and decisions can be made in this way, but I didn't look at the rules of procedure of this organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've said that already, but I want to know whether there are other ways in which decisions might be reached other than those two.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt there can be a third way if we're talking about affairs falling within the competence of this organ. Of course, in a regular situation, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. But in either of these circumstances the presidents of the member republics have a say in the making of the decision.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't look at the rules of procedure, but I assume that they participate in decision-making, because what is done by the Supreme Defence Council has to be distinguished strictly from command in the army, which is regulated by Articles 3, 4, and 5 and 6 of the law on the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to have a brief look at the constitution of Serbia, which is P855, and at Article 83. Now, you have that in front of you. If you look at 83(4), you'll see that it gives the president of the republic the power to conduct foreign relations, and paragraph (5) gives them power over the army. Can you explain the point of having these provisions in this constitution at a time when it was part of a federation which had responsibility for foreign relations and the army.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This constitution of Serbia was enacted in mid-1990, and in any case, it was enacted after clear amendments were made by some federal units to their constitutions in which they aspired to declare their own independent states, independence and sovereignty. I assume that the drafter of the Serbian constitution wanted to have a constitution in which certain affairs of state, which belonged to the federal state which was at that time in the process of disappearing, which would prepare Serbia to become an independent and sovereign state. This constitution was enacted in mid-1990, a little bit before that. In the first half of 1990. Whereas the contusion of the FRY was adopted in 1992, after this constitution of the Republic of Serbia was adopted. As I did not participate in the drafting of this constitution and I didn't live in Belgrade at that time, I cannot provide any further explanation, but these are my assumptions based on my knowledge of the situation then prevailing in Yugoslavia and the problems in the functioning of the federal state at that time, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your opinion would this give power to the president to mobilise the army within Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of Serbia, after the adoption of the federal constitution, of course not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, before the adoption of the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this constitution was adopted Serbia did not have an army of its own. It was a very difficult situation in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and many things were very unusual. So it was hard. It was unusual to see all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you are looking at the situation on the ground, and then after the FRY constitution was adopted would this have given the president of the republic power to mobilise the army? That's the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the area of defence as we saw yesterday was within the competence of the federal state. There was the army of Yugoslavia. There was a system of defence and army which was regulated by law. Serbia did not have its own army, nor did it have any legislation regulating these matters governing all this, so these provisions were not implemented and they did not give any powers to the president of the -- of Serbia because they were not in compliance with the federal constitution, and as far as I know, no republican president ever issued any orders of that kind because there was no one for him to issue them to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if this provision was -- these various provisions, and that's (4) and (5) and also (6) and (7) which are of a similar nature -- sorry, (6) and (8), which are of a similar nature, whether these were revoked once the FRY constitution was adopted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no. All I know is they were not implemented because the drafter of the constitution desisted from implementing norms which were evidently not in compliance with the federal constitution, and there were never any attempts to implement these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we now look, please, and it's on the screen, at Article 85. What is your understanding of the extent of the power of the president in light of that article?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the republic, as the norm expressly states, has the constitutional right to ask the government to put forward its views. These are not legal acts, just general political positions of the government policy concerning some issues within its competence. Beyond that, the republican government has no further obligations, and the president of the republic can do nothing de jure in relation to a government which would fail to present him with its views. But as the organs are bound to cooperate with one another, it would be quite normal for the government to put forward its views. Such norms similar to this one are not unusual in comparative law. This would resemble the French system of government from the fifth republic. It did not have that much influence in shaping systems such as that in the constitution of the USA or the one in British parliamentarianism, but it did have an influence on comparative constitutional law worldwide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this is an example that might enable the president to bring pressure to bear on the government, political pressure?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can assume that this norm could be used in that way if there was any form of disagreement between those two state organs. However, the government does not depend on the president of the republic. It depends on the majority in the national assembly and only the national assembly can vote -- can vote on no confidence in the manner that is prescribed by the legislation in relation to the government. And that's all that matters to me as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We also have on the screen at the moment Article 83(12). If we can go back to 83. You will see a very apparently wide power to conduct other affairs in accordance with the constitution. Earlier when dealing with -- I think it was the question of international negotiations, you made reference to there being no provision which prevented the president from acting. Should 83(12) be read in that way, that he is entitled to do anything as long as he is not prohibited from doing so?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke this morning about the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should have made that clear. But looking at this in light of what you said about the other constitution, should we read 83(12) as giving him similar power to do anything that is not prohibited?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 83 here it says what acts, conditionally speaking, are enacted by the president of the Republic of Serbia in carrying out his authorities. It says he can perform other tasks in compliance with this constitution. In connection with this, I can only recall that the Constitutional Court of Serbia once ruled on an attempt by the legislator to extend the competence of the president beyond the powers enumerated in the constitution. And on that occasion I think it had to do with ranks or promotions in the MUP. I can't recall specifically, but it was something like that. And the Constitutional Court held that the list of powers of the president of Serbia is a closed list and it can contain only what is stated here in the constitution and that the legislator cannot expand on this list. Therefore, that the legislator overstepped the boundaries of his authority. I didn't expect to be asked about these details, so I don't have with me now that decision and the law in question, but that was the gist of the standpoint taken by the Constitutional Court of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read the paragraph aloud to me, please, paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Conduct other affairs in accordance with the constitution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, it refers to other affairs.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which would suggest it's not confined to Article 83.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does say in accordance with the constitution, and the intention of the drafter of the constitution was to regulate the relations of the highest constitutional bodies of government, meaning the highest legislative body, the head of state and the government or cabinet on the one hand and judicial power on the other hand. And such relations in legal terms could not be expanded or reduced by the activity of the legislator, because constitutional norms, especially when it comes to competencies, cannot be understood as being open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to identify perhaps something else in the constitution that is not in 83 that he can conduct in accordance with the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I can't identify something, but a constitution is a single legal document. Sometimes there are errors in editing and norms concerning competencies can be found in more than one article of the constitution, but what matters is that they are in the constitution and they all have equal legal value. So if somewhere else there is mention of the power of the president not listed here, there's one norm regulating competency. Whether it will be technically distributed among the various articles is immaterial to a lawyer. So they all together make up a single norm. Nowhere in constitutional law is it recorded that one norm should prohibit or impinge on another or that something should be regulated with only one norm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were in Belgrade in the first half of the 1990s, in 1993 to 1995, do you accept that -- that President Milosevic was the principal power within the Republic of Serbia? As a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1995 I practically lived in Pale and only worked in Belgrade two days a week. I can go back to what I said yesterday. I cannot answer questions asking me to speculate on political power and influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm asking for your own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't tell you anything about that because I'm here as an expert who is to give his opinion on legal sources, the norms of legal sources, their meaning and their mutual connections. If you were to call me as a fact witness I might be able to testify to certain facts, but I do not feel bound to answer such questions as it is because they go beyond my role as an expert here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your role here is not confined to that of an expert. It's open to the Tribunal to ask you such questions as they consider relevant to the issues before them, and your experience of life at that time is relevant and therefore I ask you again to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to repeat that from 1993 to 1995 I spent four-fifths of my time at Pale and one-fifth in Belgrade and I was working, doing my job, looking at legal documents. I didn't really delve into who had the most influence in Serbia, whether it was Mr. Milosevic or someone else, and believe me, I can't even recall all the names of people who were holding certain positions in Serbia. I wasn't even a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia. I was not a member of any political party in Serbia. I was not participating in political life in Serbia. I had other professional and personal problems, and I cannot in all honesty respond to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And as a citizen of Yugoslavia you had no interest in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was legally recognised, and its unit, the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you had no interest in the conflict going on there which it has since been established had connections with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What conflict do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean the conflict that Republika Srpska -- or the ultimate Republika Srpska was involved in and the parts of Bosnia claimed by Serbs and occupied by Serbs. You say you had no interest in that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the status of Republika Srpska, of course I was interested in the status of Republika Srpska because I worked in one of its organs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, for example, the conflict at that time led in 1995 to the commission of what's been described as genocide in Srebrenica. You weren't interested in the conflict that ultimately led to that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we understand each other, Your Honour. First of all you asked me about what I thought about President Milosevic and his political role in Serbia, and then you went on to mention the conflict without mentioning which, so I can't actually know which conflict you're referring to. Then you went on to tell me that it was the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in which Republika Srpska was involved and then ultimately you linked me up with the genocide in Srebrenica as a concept, and then you asked me whether I was disinterested in that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I don't understand what you're actually asking me in that regard. If you're asking me what my attitude is to the events in Srebrenica, my attitude is like any humane person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. You know that very well. I'm going you about your interest in affairs in the former Yugoslavia between 1993 and 1995, and I'm curious to know what you were interested in. You just ignored any conflict that was taking place in any part of Bosnia. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does Milosevic have to do with that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not my question at the moment. I'm asking you, I'm trying to understand what it was in that part of the world you took an interest in between 1993 and 1995, and so far I've established nothing. You seem to live in a vacuum.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1995? In 1993 -- or, rather, from 1993 to 1995 I left Sarajevo at the end of April 1992 after an assassination attempt against my family. I attended the peace conference in Brussels on the 29th of April, 1992, when I don't know who tried to kill my family. My family went to Belgrade with the last bus. It escaped on the last bus, and I return to Belgrade from Brussels to take over my family. I took my family to Igalo. I spent some time there. And then I was invited by the organs of Republika Srpska, I spent a short there. And then I set off to take part in the peace negotiations which were being conducted at that time. I took part as a legal advisor to the delegation of the Republika Srpska at the negotiations in Geneva which were conducted in 1993 -- rather, 1992 and 1993, and the working group for Bosnia and Herzegovina, a negotiating group in New York, later on there was a lot of that kind of thing. I worked in the ministry of Republika Srpska sometime from -- or, rather, I was at Pale more than travelling around from 1990 -- well, the end of 1993 sometime, and of course I worked for the organs of Republika Srpska in my professional field, and my interests were, if you're asking me, that the war should finally be over so that life could get back to normal if that was possible. So if that's what you're asking me, go ahead, what I thought then and I'll do my best to answer to the best of my recollections if that's what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's against that background that I'm asking you whether in your experience Milosevic had considerable power in Serbia and was viewed as a person who had power at that time by the public in general.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any experience with that. Let me repeat, I wasn't living in Serbia at the time. I happened to see Mr. Milosevic two or three times in my life at negotiations in Geneva and Brussels and that's all the experience I have of Mr. Milosevic. Other meetings with Mr. Milosevic, I did not have, so my experience with his method of work is something that I actually do not possess. I have no knowledge about what the structure of political decision-making was in Serbia at the time, what the perception was by the public, this public or that public in one way or another. I really can't say. I don't know. I had too many of my own duties and obligations, family, professional, and so on to be able to spend time on things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Some of the experiences of your family are such that one might expect you to have a particular interest in events in the region in general.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat.
