I did have an interest in seeing that my family survives and that my children can develop as normally as possible and to take part in Republika Srpska and the events there and to bring about a peaceful end. That was what I was interested in. Those were my interests, and that's -- it exhausted my working potential. I don't know what other interests you mean and what it was you think I should have followed and formed my own conclusions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, lastly I want to look at P1737 and Article 9. This is the Law on Internal Affairs, and you'll see that it provides that: "At the request of the national assembly and the president of the republic," that's the Republic of Serbia, "the minister must submit a report on the work of the ministry of the interior and on the security situation in the republic." Are you aware of any controversy surrounding the meaning of that provision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, truly not. I did not take into account this law in my expert report because it didn't have anything to do with my subjects. As for the controversies in political or state life or legal life of Serbia, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I perhaps have made an assumption here that should be clarified, but I take it you are familiar with the constitution of the Republic of Serbia of 1990.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not look at the law governing internal affairs because it didn't have anything to do with my expert report. Your Honour, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now I can ask you this question: The view has been expressed to us that that provision, Article 9, is unconstitutional. What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but when was this law enacted? Because I really didn't analyse it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can probably find out by going to the beginning of it. I don't have a hard copy in my hand. Apparently we don't have the beginning of it either. However, it's been presented as current.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's been --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was amended in 1996 -- but the interpreter did not hear the year. 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, it was amended in 1991, did you say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in 1996. Yes. It was enacted in 1991. Perhaps it was amended in 1991 as well and in 1999 as it said in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what we have is the amended version of 1996. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you agree with the view expressed that it is unconstitutional?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please -- can we scroll down so that I can see Article 9 again, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the English as well, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that that is unconstitutional because it's not any kind of document or act being enacted because with respect to the army there would have to be a legal document. This is just an obligation for mutual information which is now placed into a legal form which does not upset the relationships between the president of the government and the -- of the republic and the government. So it could not be considered to be expanding competencies. Expanding competencies would imply authorisation with respect to the enactment of legal documents. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The view was expressed to us based on there being no provision in the constitution obliging of the Ministry of Interior to report.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the role of the president according to the constitution of 1990, the President of Serbia, that is, I don't think that this is not in keeping with the constitution, because organs, the various bodies, should cooperate amongst themselves. And after a report the president has no competencies either with respect to the ministry of the interior or the government because the government depends on -- in existence of the national assembly and the legal character of its legal documents depends on the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, Mr. Hannis, does anything arise out of that for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There was one topic. It had to do with the powers of President Milosevic vis-a-vis the MUP, and if I may inquire about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, you recall yesterday we gave you a hard copy of a document to read during the break. That's our Exhibit P2166 about a meeting of the operations interdepartmental staff for the suppression or combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, and you -- you pointed out the fact that at the end of that document there are merely some conclusions reached, that there was no decision and you didn't see anything in the nature of an order coming from President Milosevic, and I think the gist of your comment was that therefore your view was that this body was really sort of in the nature of a consultative body that the president met with to address these issues. Is that fair to characterise your conclusion that way?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. Of course with the proviso that I based my conclusion on the basis of documents, and the one I saw yesterday was -- I had just a very brief chance of looking at it and I did so later last night. So the arguments that I put forth were properly interpreted by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment please, I have an objection to make in the way in which Mr. Hannis formulated his question. I don't remember that the witness accepted that it was a consultative body yesterday. I think he spoke about a consultative meeting. That is my memory of witness testimony yesterday, whereas my colleague Mr. Hannis on page 35, line 18, put it that he spoke about a constitutive body yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Consultative body, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I said a meeting at which consultations held. I wasn't wary enough when the Prosecutor put his question but this is an opportunity for me to step up my awareness and wariness. I didn't say that it was a consultative body. I said that there was no such body in those organs but that it was a meeting at which an exchange of information took place, at which consultations took place, to refer to what I said in my answer yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Hannis will be content to accept all of that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to show you Exhibit 4D100. We'll put it on the screen. I know you've not seen this before. This is a document from General Pavkovic who was commander of the Pristina Corps at that time on the 22nd of July, 1998. This is to his 3rd Army command, and we will have the B/C/S in a moment. And he's referencing a meeting with President Milosevic on the 21st of July, 1998, where he says: "An order was given to implement the plan for combatting terrorist forces in Kosovo ... the plan envisages the participation of the MUP and Pristina Corps units in blocking Junik and Jasic villages," et cetera. Now, keep that in mind. I want to show you another document, 4D101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to the use of these two documents. I think that this line of questioning that Mr. Hannis has just started goes beyond the topics you dealt with in your examination. These documents have not been announced and I don't think they are in any way linked to the expert report by Professor Lukic and his personal knowledge which would emanate from yesterday's questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- this line of questioning arises out of questions Your Honour asked the witness about the constitutional powers of President Milosevic vis-a-vis the MUP. You asked questions regarding what President Milosevic did in the negotiations in the October agreements and about reducing the forces of the MUP in the area. You asked him about the MUP and the border issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the document you're about to refer to relates to both the president and the MUP, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there something further you want to say, Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd just like to add that this is a document of the Pristina Corps, which mean communication between the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The next one is 4D101. Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, it's clear to us that this does arise out of the questions posed from the Bench, and the link is clear and therefore we will allow these documents to be used and the questions -- the line of examination to be followed. Please draw to my attention any particular prejudice you feel is caused to you that may require us to grant some remedy, for example, an adjournment or whatever if you think there is something else that needs to be investigated or for any other reason. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This next document is -- thank you. This document is 4D101 which is dated the 23rd of July, 1998. This is also from General Pavkovic to the command of the 3rd Army. You see in the first full paragraph, it says, "Implementation of the second stage of the plan to eliminate terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija provides for the engagement of organs of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the necessary units of the Pristina Corps". Skipping down to the last sentence he's saying to his commander General Samardzic: "You have been briefed on this plan as the whole several times, the last time at the briefing with the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 21 July 1998 when the order was given to commence implementation of the plan." I'll hand you hard copies of both those documents. And then the last thing I want to do is refer you to some testimony of Dusan Matkovic, who testified on -- who testified for us on the 30th of August, 2007, and he made reference to a meeting with General -- with President Milosevic on the 20th or 21st of July, 1998. He described those attending as including President Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, himself, Mr. Minic, Mr. Andjelkovic, General Samardzic, General Dimitrijevic, General Perisic, General Pavkovic from the VJ, the minister of the interior for Serbia minister Stojiljkovic, some other MUP generals including Djordjevic and Lukic, and he describes what was discussed at the meeting, and if I can get the exact reference he tells us at page 14636 that there was a proposal for a plan of anti-terrorist struggle to be adopted which would consist of several stages and the proposal was made and elaborated upon by General Pavkovic, and at line 24, page 14636, the question: "So General Pavkovic proposed or presented this plan and did you all agree upon it?" His answer was: "It was not a question of the three or four of us politicians agreeing. President Milosevic said that this plan was adopted and that this -- it had to be implemented, that it was the duty of the army." So was it within President Milosevic's constitutional powers and authority to command or order that the MUP be engaged, the MUP of the Republic of Serbia be engaged in anti-terrorist operations with the VJ? Can you answer that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Not on the basis of this time -- the time I have, the speed at which I have to read this. This is all factual news to me and I can't find my way around this, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of anyplace in the constitution where the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had the authority to order or direct the engagement of Republic of Serbia MUP police to engage in anti-terrorist activities, and if so, tell me where in the constitution it says that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An express provision about that doesn't exist anywhere. I cannot find it specifically according to how you put it and to the best of my recollections, but you can gain an impression and conclusion if you look at all the documents which I'm not able to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Zecevic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know it's no simple matter for us -- for you to ad hoc assess the constitutionality of provisions that you haven't actually had a chance to look at, but a moment ago I'm sure you'll remember being asked by His Honour is something with respect to Article 9 of the law governing the internal affairs. P1737 is the document number. The Judge stated that there had been testimony here that this provision was unconstitutional or that might be unconstitutional since, of course, the constitutionality is something that the constitutional court will determine?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you of your answer regarding the constitutionality of the articles contained in the law on the ranks of the personnel of the Ministry of Interior of Serbia. You said that you could not recall what law this pertained to, what regulations this pertained to but that you thought that was the one, and you said that as far as you could recall the statement of reasons supplied by the Constitutional Court attached to its decision was the following: The constitutional court held the view that the powers of the president of Serbia were defined only by the constitution and that laws cannot expand them. Is that what you said? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I paraphrased the decision of the constitutional court of Serbia by memory. It was passed quite a long time ago and it's a long time since I read it, so this is really a very vague recollection on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, as an expert in constitutional law you studied the constitution of Serbia, but would you agree with the position taken there that the powers of the President of Serbia could only be defined by the constitution and could not be defined by the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but bearing in mind the caveat that I put in place because you're asking me to make decisions after four or five minutes and constitutional courts have days to deliberate. So this is the caveat that I have put in place. If you have to make an -- give an answer in one minute, my distinction was that legal acts that might affect the position of other persons or organs cannot be passed. That is the way I understood it. If the president of the republic could on the basis of this provision affect the mandate of the minister of the interior or if he could pass any legal acts, in my view that would constitute impermissible expansion of his powers. Of course that is the way I understand it, the way I interpret it in the time that I was given, one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more claim, Professor. If I understood your position properly, you considered that this provision contained in Article 9 of the Law on Internal Affairs, because there were no consequences, it could be considered constitutional but not on the basis of the fact that such powers are not vested in the president by the constitution but by a law which is not permissible. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion is based only on the fact that these are not powers to exercise power or to enact any legal acts based on this provision. I also conclude that there are no elements that would disturb the relations between the president of the republic and the government of the republic. That is what I have been able to come up with in the three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when we read -- just a moment, please. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Petrovic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor Lukic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give evidence and to assist the Tribunal. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can deal with certain other matters at this stage. Mr. Hannis, I understand you want to raise an issue relating to the length of final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. My understanding is pursuant to the practice direction applicable that was passed, I think in 2005, there's a word limitation of 60.000 words for the closing brief. Given the number of accused in this case, this is one of the first larger multi-defendant cases to come to this stage, we -- our best judgement is that we would be asking for somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100 or 120.000 words. I want to bring that to your attention at the earliest possible date so whatever your ruling is, we can adjust accordingly and make our best efforts to comply with your requirements and try and do an efficient job as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any Defence counsel have any submission to make on this topic? Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The only thing I would request - no objection to that request - is that perhaps we could have some latitude as well. We may exceed the 60.000 words, too. We're not a point of course where we know how many words we'll need, but everything together, footnotes and text, it's all calculated to determine the length of the brief and we don't want to find ourselves caught a few thousand words short or space for a few thousand words or so. We'll do our best to be concise, of course, but this is a huge case with six accused, and I think our brief may very well exceed what 60.000 words amounts to in pages. So we ask for your indulgence there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Fila, we gave an indication that when Mr. Djakovic gives evidence that we would expect the Defence to cross-examine followed by the Prosecution, and you were anxious to make submissions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me paint it in a different way. Whenever Mr. Hannis went beyond the time that was envisaged for his cross-examination I did not object to it because he did a good job. Well, with some exceptions when he would put -- try to put things in like a body instead of a meeting and minutes instead of notes. So he did a good job. That was his reward. But if the Prosecution does not call an expert on constitutional law and you examine this witness for three and a half hours, because the Prosecution did not do its job properly, all the court witnesses that you called were called because the Prosecution did not do its job properly, and now you're punishing me by making me cross-examine the witness before the Prosecution. I am supposed to be rewarded for proposing that this be done instead of being punished by -- for being forced to ask questions in this order. This would not be in the spirit of justice and fairness to have the Defence ask questions before the Prosecution because you know the Defence has the last word before any court, and I am really glad that you admitted that I was right when I insisted that a constitutional expert should be called and those other witnesses. So thank you very much. I'm glad to see I have been right at least in one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have a position on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's a matter clearly within your discretion. In terms of judicial economy I would suggest there's a possibility that if the six Defence counsel go first, given some of the competing interests that I perceive to exist in this case and in particular with regard to this witness, there's a chance I may not have any questions left to ask after all. That's the only comment I have to make. Otherwise, if you want me to go first I'll go first but then that's six of them to deal with the questions I raised versus one of me to deal with questions six of them raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may. The second part of my memo pertains to this: We can make a deal about that and here Mr. Hannis is right and I accept that, that we can do this time schedule. We can do this in such a way that the Prosecution does not feel that it's been prejudiced because they would be asking questions for one day and we would be asking questions for three days. And if you ask questions in such great detail of Djakovic as you have now, I don't think I will have any questions, but if the Prosecution is bothered by that, you can set a time limit for us. They had a time limit of 30 minutes and they never went below two hours. So that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps a sweeping generalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It was just a joke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There remains the issue of what's outstanding, just to identify what it is, and we need to adjourn before we deal with that, but we don't need to adjourn for an hour. If it's convenient to parties and to the other support staff and interpreters, we can adjourn more briefly and return to deal with that and that would give us, I suspect is, a finish by the usual 1.45 time scale. Now, before I go off to sort of finalise the agenda of what we perceive as the outstanding issues, is there any other matter that you wish to raise that we can deal with now? Very well. We will resume at 1.15 and hopefully finish by 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the Prosecution to submit a final brief of up to, if necessary, 100.000 words, and will allow the Defence in each instance, if necessary, up to 70.000. The order of examination of Chamber witnesses will be that the Prosecutor will precede the Defence but will have an opportunity of further cross-examination should the need arise out of questions posed by Defence counsel. The outstanding matters that we are anxious to identify to ensure they're not lost sight of and are completed prior to the close of evidence in this case and in accordance with orders already made are as follows: The VJ rules of service, the Pavkovic Defence have now to upload the 1996 version with a new exhibit number. That's to be done by Wednesday, and the parties have to be -- sorry, the Chamber, the parties, and CLSS should be notified immediately that's done; the sooner the better. 6D1615, that's the law on the cooperation of Serbia and Montenegro with the ICTY, there is now a translation of that document available. If there is no objection from the Prosecution, that could now be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Yesterday we ordered the Lukic Defence to upload a revised report for Professor Lukic. That's 2D393. We imposed no deadline, but could that be done by close of business today, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that was the Sainovic Defence as it's there witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this has already been done this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will allow the revised report to be substituted for the original. Further translation issues, Mr. Hannis: 5D1114, which is an order of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade command, and 5D1428, a report on the activities of the Ministry of the Interior of the 27th of October 1998 to 25 January 1999, and 5D1459, the telephone list of the Decani OUP. There are now translations for these. Do you want time to consider them or can we admit them?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I advise your legal officer by e-mail this afternoon? I just need to take a quick look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. We might -- if there is no objection, on Monday we can make a further oral order dealing with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I remind the Lazarevic Defence that documents denied in the original bar table motion because they were not translated have to be submitted with translations by the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, and I have checked recently with my associates. There are just two brief documents that have yet to be translated, I think five or six pages in total, and we received the promise that they would be translated by Monday, 10.00 or 11.00 a.m., and I think that we will be able to submit all translations before the deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, add to your list in relation to translation 6D344 and 6D345. The Pavkovic OTP interview, parties were discussing corrections to that and a new version will have to be submitted if corrections are agreed upon. What is the state of play on that one, Mr. Aleksic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I can't assist you with that. I think that my colleague Mr. Ackerman was in communication with Mr. Hannis, but I don't think that there are any problems. We will deal with that in the course of this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I have to speak to Mr. Ackerman. I don't know where we stand on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to know the position by Monday on that one, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've expected a revised translation of P1974 from the Prosecution. That's an order relating to Cicevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm advised it's been done and uploaded already, Your Honour, but we haven't filed the notification. We'll do that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The revised translation will be admitted and no filing is required, simply an intimation now from your case manager to the court officer of the ID number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, P2804 has to be resubmitted to CLSS. I think we allowed until Monday for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it has been resubmitted to them, but -- yeah. I'm advised that it's due back Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I remind the Lukic Defence that the two video clips used with Zlatkovic 6D16 -- sorry, yeah, 6D1633 and 6D295 compilations of what was played in court have to be compiled and submitted by Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That will -- that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Add to your list, Mr. Hannis, 6D1619. That's a map for which there is now a translation. That is described, Mr. Aleksic, as a map of Kosmac, K-o-s-m-a-c. Is that an accurate expression?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kosmac, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it should say. Thank you. 6D612 which are reports from Prizren SUP, by Monday a new B/C/S version of that exhibit including only the portions corresponding to the pages that have been translated is to be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's already uploaded. We're just doing the notification to give what pages are actually part of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can give that notification directly to the court officer and we will allow substitution for -- the new one for the current 6D612.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The revised or amended version of the report of Branimir Jokic was to be tendered by Monday as Exhibit 1D743. Whose responsible for dealing with that? Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are. We will -- it's coming, Your Honour. It will be filed by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there's a Prosecution motion to admit the identity papers of the witness Sadiku, which is P3141. If there's no objection to that motion, then we can deal with that here. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have a reply that's being filed today. Today's the last day -- pardon me, a response not a reply, being filed in that. There is an issue with the translation of one document. That's a minor issue that CLSS should be able to handle. And then we have a further submission, I believe, presenting one other further document that goes along with that ought to also to be admitted wholesale. So there will not be an objection to the filing -- to admission per se, just with the correction of a translation issue and addressing another relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall deal with that either in writing or orally once we've had an opportunity to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We invited the Milutinovic Defence to provide any additional information that might be of assistance to the Chamber in relation to the law of the army of Yugoslavia and the question of how there were three paragraphs in one version and two in another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're working on that. I think the deadline was Wednesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I simply draw it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It will it be filed by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was similar -- the explanation offered was similar to the one you get at the station that the train you're going for is late because of the late arrival of the preceding train. We need more of an explanation for that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. We'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are motions outstanding in our hands. There's a motion relating to the Lukic OTP interview. There will be a decision on that issued in writing shortly. It will be today or Monday. There is a request from the Prosecution in relation to the witness statements of a number of Lukic witnesses where the translations were not entirely completed by CLSS and a decision on that will be issued shortly. Mr. Ivetic, you've filed a corrigendum to your motion, your bar table motion, about 6D1644, which is a reply from the Serbian authorities saying that there are no original maps of specified anti-terrorist actions in the military archives, and you seek to withdraw that letter. Now, what is going on on this one? Because we were keen to see originals if they exist. If you withdraw the letter and the paragraph of your motion, that would suggest, possibly suggest, that they do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a long-standing debate I've been having with the authorities and the answers that I get from them. It was my understanding that what had been reported to me is not necessarily what's in the -- the response that was received and since I didn't have a translation of that handy I went upon what others had told me and I'm told that it's not exactly as we -- as we this thought so that there might have been another response later somewhat drawing back from that or giving other information. So I really don't know and that's why we needed to -- I could not make an affirmative affirmation at that time relative to that and that's why we did the corrigendum and I think there was one other document that went in erroneously that wasn't relevant that also did not have a translation and I forget. I think there might even have been a third and fourth document that are not related to that issue but which also were erroneously included in the bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you now submitted all you intend to submit on this point? Or are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On that point, yes, that's all that I have at present that I can -- that I can -- with the -- everything in the bar table motion is complete with the corrigendum, and I do have, of course, from -- I don't know if you want to go into it now but for the bar table motion there are a couple other open points, I know, that we could go into. I have been in contact with the Rule 70 provider and hope to have some further information regarding those documents shortly. They were working on getting the approvals for the same and we should get hopefully some word on that shortly. There's the issue of 6D2. As Your Honours know, we have one document that was from that witness. I have not yet received a positive response on the other document that the Trial Chamber sought from that witness, without going into further details in open court. Essentially that document has not been located by the said witness at this time. And there was one dispatch of the RJB that Your Honours had sought that was referenced in one document, that was 6D770. This dispatch to the RJB was referenced on the 28th of February, 2008, during the testimony of Mr. Dujkovic, and at that time the Trial Chamber said that it would be worthwhile to try and get that document. We have now received that document and I believe there's ban motion already filed last night asking for admission -- or asking for the same to be admitted once the translation is completed. That would be 6D1667 that's the April 19, 1999 dispatch, the RJB in connection with the testimony of Mr. Dujkovic that the Trial Chamber had at that time directed us to try and locate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a brief document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Two pages, I think, two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you ask for it to be translated as matter of urgency, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to raise with you 6D2. You've dealt with that. On the question we were discussing 6D1644. All I can do is note what you say. In relation to police log 6D614, you have been asked to explain the delay on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, and I believe we were told to do that by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tuesday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Tuesday, that's correct, and that will be done I'm working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Additional information is required of that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I think it was transcript references for the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, in general terms your bar table motion does contain a number of documents which are not translated. What is the position with the translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, we are working trying to exert all of our resources on that both through CLSS and through our -- the approved in-house translator approved by the Registry for those documents that CLSS cannot handle due to their -- to their constraints in terms of the capacity. We are trying to get as many of those done because we believe that they are essential and we're trying to get the shorter ones and the more essential ones to be given priority as we have throughout the proceedings. I don't have anything specific to report at this time. We could give more information next week if I have the weekend to try and make a few phone calls and inquiries as to where we stand. As Your Honours have noted, we've been filing translations I think pretty much on a daily basis as they come in, so we're trying do get as much of that under control as soon as possible sooner rather than later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we are approaching the stage where a line is going to be drawn, and not a line in the sand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just finally going back to the translations of the witness statements where they were not entirely translated by CLSS, our understanding was that the revised translations would be available by today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, is a matter beyond my control. That's in CLSS's hands. We did provide them both the -- everything essentially, we provided them everything as they had requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The day is young.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But there's no reason to doubt that they will be available today so please do what you can to ensure that these are filed all with a view to reducing the outstanding issues so far as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed. As soon as we get any translation either from CLSS or anyone else, we upload that day, so that's why we have the multiple filings for admission of documents that were MFI or otherwise didn't have translations. We'll do the same with these with the caveat that I think with the statements we'll send courtesy copies rather than waiting for a notification and going through the filing system given the weekend if in fact something is brought back to us today by CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Visnjic, you seemed to have raised a matter. Do you wish to raise it in court or -- I understand you've communicated with -- with the legal staff about one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'll be satisfied with a written response. We look upon it as a technical matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in the circumstances we'll look at what's said first of all and give you a response either in writing or orally, but it will be a fairly quick one. I hope I've identified all that's outstanding. We can now --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. May I make a request to the Lukic Defence team in connection with the pending bar table motion. If it would be possible to get a Word copy of their document because they're numerous and not all exhibits are always listed in numerical order or date order. In filing my response it would be helpful to me if I could have a Word document to work from if that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That a problem, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ought not to be. I don't know what the format was. Oh, it's probably submitted in .tif or .pdf. I could do that to -- I would send it to everyone, I think, instead of just the Prosecution in case there is anyone else that's doing a response I'll send it to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall now adjourn until Monday at 9.00, court number III.
